column4: Pixel-art texture in the style of 1990s Build-engine games (Duke Nukem 3D, Blood, Redneck Rampage): a flat orthographic straight-on view filling the whole canvas edge to edge with no perspective, no background, no shadow, chunky pixels, low saturation, grimy, dense detail, no readable text, no border, no watermark. The whole left side of a 1980s Czechoslovak Skoda 1203 post van of the Ceska posta in 1998, straight side view filling the canvas: a boxy small forward-control van with a short sloping nose on the left, a sliding side door with a small window, painted in the faded Czech post yellow-orange with a dark blue band along the bottom and a dark blue round post-horn emblem on the side, chrome trim, black steel wheels with small hubcaps, mud splashed up the lower edge, a dent and rust bubbles above the rear wheel arch.

Pixel-art game character sprite in exactly the same style as the reference image: same pixel size, same palette, same grainy noisy shading, front view, full body standing, feet touching the bottom edge, character centred and filling about 90% of the height. A thin Czech postman in his forties in 1998: a grey-blue post office uniform jacket buttoned up with a small dark blue post-horn badge on the chest, grey-blue trousers, a grey-blue peaked cap with a post-horn badge, a worn brown leather post bag on a strap across his body, black shoes, a drooping moustache, holding a brown clipboard in one hand. His face is a little too still and his smile does not reach the eyes, something faintly off about him. Grainy, noisy, unsettling like a found photograph, never cheerful. Background must be flat solid pure magenta #FF00FF everywhere around it, no ground shadow, no floor, no text, no border, no watermark.

A hand-painted close-up scene for an early 1990s DOS adventure game (Sierra, LucasArts, SimAnt event screens), 320x240 VGA pixel art, 256 colours, chunky dithered pixels, low warm office light, seen from where you stand behind a worn wooden reception counter, filling the whole canvas, no readable text, no UI, no border, no watermark. Across the counter a Czech postman in a grey-blue uniform jacket and peaked cap leans in, his face cut off by the top edge of the picture, only his moustache and chin showing, one hand holding down a brown clipboard he has pushed across to you. On the clipboard, large and flat in the lower middle of the picture, a pale green post office delivery slip with printed boxes and ruled lines and one big empty white box at its bottom for a signature (no readable letters anywhere), a cheap ballpoint pen on a string beside it, a rubber stamp and an ink pad at the edge of the counter, the dim office behind him.

On the counter in front of you a big heavy parcel: a cardboard box wrapped in brown paper and tied crosswise with coarse string, a handwritten address label, blue and white post stickers and a red fragile sticker (no readable letters), a corner dented. Behind it the grey-blue sleeve and hand of the postman just letting go of it, the dim office behind.

A scanned photograph from a cheap 1998 Czech computer shop catalogue, slightly blurry, faded colours, visible JPEG artefacts and scanner noise: a used beige 15-inch CRT computer monitor on its swivel foot, three-quarter view, the screen dark grey and slightly reflective, a coiled grey VGA cable and a black power cable in front of it, a small graphics card with two VGA sockets lying beside it, on a plain mottled grey studio background, no readable text, no logos, no border, no watermark.

The front edges of a stack of three thick old 1990s telephone directories lying flat on top of each other, seen straight from the side: the bottom one yellow, the middle one faded white, the top one yellow, their soft paper covers dog-eared and bent, the thin page edges in fine grey lines between the covers, a coffee ring stain, filling the whole canvas.
